site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: Bharata's Sandals on the Throne
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana · Aranya Kanda, Sarga 70 (Gita Press translation)
body: In the green hush of the Dandaka forest, where Rama lived as an ascetic after his exile, his brother Bharata arrived with a grieving retinue. King Dasharatha had passed away from sorrow, and Bharata, reluctantly crowned, could not bear to sit upon a throne meant for another.

When the brothers embraced beneath the trees, Bharata begged Rama to return to Ayodhya and rule. Rama gently refused, honoring his father's word. Bharata accepted his brother's resolve with a heavy but loving heart, knowing the dharma of the promise must be kept.

Taking Rama's wooden sandals as a sacred token, Bharata carried them home and placed them upon the throne of Ayodhya, ruling only as a humble servant in his brother's name. He lived as an ascetic, waiting faithfully until the exile's end, a devotion that still warms the heart.

stories.title: The Monkey's Quick Heart
body: On a sun-warmed river, a crocodile befriended a monkey who feasted daily on the sweet figs of a nearby tree. Each evening the kind-hearted monkey tossed the ripest fruit down to his unlikely companion below, and their quiet friendship ripened with the season.

But the crocodile's wife grew greedy when she heard the tale, scheming to eat the monkey's heart, certain that one fed on figs must keep a fig-heart inside. The crocodile, torn between loyalty and love, lured his friend onto his back with promises of a feast in his own home.

Halfway across the deep water, the crocodile confessed his wife's cruel wish. Calm and clever, the monkey sighed that his heart still hung on the fig tree branch. Believing him, the crocodile turned back, and the grateful monkey leapt unharmed to shore, his gentle wits saving the day.

stories.title: The Blue Jackal's Brief Crown
body: In the old tales of the Panchatantra, a jackal fleeing hounds tumbled into a vat of indigo dye and climbed out shining blue. The forest animals, who had never seen such a color, bowed low before him, believing a strange new king had arrived. Puffed with pride, he ruled over lion and rabbit alike.

Yet one moonlit night the wild jackals raised their howling cry, and he could not stop himself from answering with his own rough voice. The court gasped, for they knew at once that no king of legend ever howled. Bowed and tear-streaked, he slipped back into the trees, his borrowed crown gone with the dye.

He found his old place among the dogs who had chased him, and the forest settled again into its honest music. The story smiles on him, for a disguise may dazzle for a while, but the true self, like a faithful song, always finds its way home.

stories.title: Agni Returns Sita and the Bow
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana · Yuddha Kanda, Sarga 100 (Gita Press translation)
body: After Ravana fell and Sita was restored to Rama, the gods and sages gathered to honor the victorious prince. The air shimmered with celebration, and the worlds grew still in gratitude.

From the flames came Agni, the fire-god, who had long kept Sita safe in his tender care when she was cast out. He brought her gently back into Rama's presence, her spirit untouched, pure and steadfast as his honored wife.

Bowing low in homage, Agni then presented to Rama the divine bow of Vishnu, which he had guarded through the ages. Rama accepted it with quiet joy, and the ancient vow made in another birth was finally fulfilled.

stories.title: Ahalya Blooms From Stone
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana · Bala Kanda, Sarga 49 (Gita Press translation)
body: On the road through the forest with sage Vishvamitra, young Rama paused at Gautama's quiet hermitage. There, where Ahalya had once lived as the sage's wife, a pale stone lay still in the sun, a long curse making her seem no more than a rock beside the path.

Where every traveler would have seen only stone, the pure-hearted prince saw Ahalya herself waiting within. At Vishvamitra's gentle urging, Rama bowed and touched the rock with his foot, and the heavy curse of years fell away like dust in the morning light.

Ahalya stepped forth, restored to her natural form, her eyes bright with relief. She folded her hands to Rama in gratitude, then turned home at last to Gautama and her own life, renewed by a single merciful touch.
